expected_title: High Altitude Aerodynamic Reflectors To Counter Climate Change
abstract: The warming of the atmosphere by net radiative forcing is now estimated to exceed 2.92 Watts per square meter of Earth’s surface. Present eﬀorts to reduce emissions of greenhouse gases and waste heat are insuﬃcient to reduce the rate of increase of radiative forcing, let alone reverse it. We discuss one implementation of an incremental, reversible and controlled concept to directly reduce heat input to the atmosphere. Swarms of thin reﬂective sheets are aerodynamically ﬂoated and controlled above 28 kilometers altitude using solar-powered electric-propelled tractor wings. The swarms drift with the summer latitudes year-round. They stay well above controlled airspace even through the longest nocturnal altitude loss of equatorial crossing. Building on prior work, wind tunnel tests study passive stabilization of thin sheets. The sheet is restrained using two edge rails and aft control surface mounted on canted vertical ﬁns. The deployment process is updated. The sheet angle of attack has to be raised to counter wing suction. Means of distributing sheet loading are studied. Passive sheet stabilization is demonstrated, with 20 micron shrink-wrap plastic, and 175-micron Mylar sheets surviving dynamic pressures an order of magnitude higher than the design cruise condition. Scaling surface imperfections is a hurdle in proving drag predictions in these wind tunnel tests at full- scale Reynolds number. The second part of the paper derives and proposes an equivalence in carbon credits between reduction of atmospheric greenhouse gases, and avoidance of heat input to the atmosphere. The proposed architecture passes all known objections warning against Climate Engineering.
